title: Lambda Expressions
description: Lambda syntax, functional interfaces from java.util.function, and how lambdas capture variables.
objectives: Write lambda expressions with various parameter/body forms
Use the core java.util.function interfaces: Predicate, Consumer, Function, Supplier
Understand effectively-final variable capture in lambdas

content.heading: Lambda Syntax
content.body: A lambda expression is a concise, inline implementation of a functional interface's single abstract method: (parameters) -> expression, or (parameters) -> { statements; return value; } for a multi-statement body. Parameter types are usually inferred from context and can be omitted: (a, b) -> a + b. A single parameter's parentheses are optional: x -> x * x. Lambdas replace much of the verbosity of anonymous inner classes for simple, single-method implementations, while compiling down to a similar underlying mechanism.

content.heading: java.util.function and Variable Capture
content.body:
java.util.function provides a standard set of general-purpose functional interfaces so you rarely need to declare your own: Predicate<T> (a boolean-returning test: T -> boolean), Function<T, R> (a transformation: T -> R), Consumer<T> (an action with no return value: T -> void), and Supplier<T> (a value producer taking no arguments: () -> T). These are the building blocks behind much of the Stream API's fluent, functional-style method chaining.

A lambda can reference local variables from its enclosing scope, but only if they are effectively final — assigned once and never reassigned afterward (even without the explicit final keyword). This mirrors Python's closure-capture behavior conceptually, but Java enforces the effectively-final rule at compile time rather than allowing (and sometimes surprising you with) mutation of a captured variable.

content.explanation: Each java.util.function interface models a distinct shape: a test (Predicate), a transformation (Function), an action (Consumer), and a producer (Supplier). factor is captured by the scale lambda because it's effectively final — never reassigned.

keyPoints: (params) -> expression is the core lambda syntax, implementing a functional interface's single method
Predicate<T>, Function<T,R>, Consumer<T>, Supplier<T> are the standard general-purpose functional interfaces
Lambdas can only capture effectively-final local variables from their enclosing scope
Lambdas underpin much of the Stream API's method-chaining style
commonMistakes: Trying to reassign a local variable that a lambda has captured, causing a compile error
Reaching for a custom functional interface when a standard one (Predicate, Function, etc.) already fits
Writing an overly long, multi-statement lambda body where a named method reference or regular method would be clearer
